questions.q: Why is a RAG pipeline best understood primarily as a data-access system rather than purely an AI feature?
options: Because it is really a document-retrieval system — chunking, embedding, similarity search, and access control — with a model summarizing the results at the end
Because RAG pipelines never involve a language model at any stage
Because vector databases are not real databases and have no access-control concerns
Because retrieval only happens after the model has already generated its answer
questions.explain: Underneath the natural-language interface, RAG is document retrieval — who can see which chunks, and what happens when untrusted retrieved content reaches the model — with generation added at the end.

questions.q: What is wrong with running a similarity search against the full vector index and then filtering out unauthorized results afterward, in application code?
options: Nothing — post-query filtering is the recommended production pattern for RAG access control
It is wrong only because it is slower than filtering during the query
It is unreliable: if top-k results are dominated by unauthorized documents, filtering afterward can leave nothing relevant, or a filtering bug can leak a result before anyone notices
It is wrong because vector stores do not support metadata at all
questions.explain: Post-filtering is the vector-search equivalent of running a SQL query with no WHERE clause and trusting the application layer to hide unauthorized rows afterward — it's structurally unreliable, not just slow.

questions.q: What does pushing authorization into the vector-store query itself (pre-query filtering) achieve?
options: It allows the system prompt to enforce access control instead of the database
It ensures a document the user cannot access is never eligible to be returned as a result in the first place, rather than being removed after the fact
It makes the client responsible for deciding which documents it is allowed to see
It removes the need for any access-control metadata on indexed chunks
questions.explain: Attaching ACL metadata at index time and requiring every query to include a server-side filter scoped to the authenticated user's permitted IDs means unauthorized chunks are excluded from the search itself, the same way row-level security scopes a SQL query.

questions.q: Why should retrieved chunks in a RAG pipeline be treated as untrusted content rather than trusted instructions?
options: Because vector stores automatically strip all text formatting from indexed content
Because retrieval only returns numerical embeddings, never text
Because retrieved chunks are always encrypted and therefore unreadable by the model

Because retrieved chunks can contain crafted, instruction-like phrasing — the same indirect-prompt-injection pattern from Chapter 2 — introduced through documents like uploads, scraped pages, or support tickets
questions.explain: Any content that entered the index from an uploaded, scraped, or forwarded source is untrusted the same way indirect prompt injection sources are — a chunk can contain phrasing crafted to be read as an instruction rather than reference material.

questions.q: Where should the access-control filter value (such as a user's group IDs) used in a retrieval query come from?
options: From the vector store's default configuration, which applies the same filter to every user
From the authenticated user's server-side session, never from a client-supplied or prompt-supplied value
From the retrieved document's own metadata as written by whoever uploaded it
From a parameter embedded in the user's prompt, since that is simplest to implement
questions.explain: Building the filter from a client- or prompt-controlled value creates an authorization bypass — the retrieval-stage equivalent of prompt injection. The filter must be derived from the authenticated session on the server.
